title: Holy Bread at Nob and Feigned Madness at Gath
summary: Alone and unarmed, David comes to the priest Ahimelech at Nob and, claiming to be on a secret mission for the king, receives the consecrated bread of the Presence and the sword of Goliath. Doeg the Edomite, one of Saul's servants, sees it all. David then flees to Achish, the Philistine king of Gath, but when Achish's servants recognize him as the hero of Israel's victory song, he pretends to be insane and is sent away.
story: At the end of chapter 20 David and Jonathan parted, and David left Saul's world for good. Chapter 21 shows how low that exile begins. The anointed king arrives at a sanctuary alone, hungry, and without a weapon, and then seeks refuge in the very Philistine city Goliath came from, carrying Goliath's sword. Both stops go badly. At Nob, David's deception will lead in the next chapter to the massacre of the priests, and at Gath his fame nearly gets him killed. The chapter shows David at his most vulnerable and his most resourceful, and it sets up one of the darkest episodes in Saul's reign.
historical:
Nob was a town of priests close to Jerusalem; Isaiah 10:32 places it within sight of the city, on the route of an army approaching from the north. After the destruction of Shiloh, which many scholars infer from the events of chapter 4 and from Jeremiah 7:12-14, the descendants of Eli appear to have served at Nob, where the ephod and bread of the Presence were kept. Ahimelech was a great-grandson of Eli, probably a brother of the Ahijah of 14:3, or else the same man under another name.

Gath was one of the five chief Philistine cities, identified with Tell es-Safi. Achish, its king, appears again in chapters 27 to 29, where David serves him as a vassal. The heading of Psalm 56 connects that psalm with the Philistines seizing David in Gath, and the heading of Psalm 34 connects it with David pretending madness before Abimelech, which many take to be a title or alternative name for the Philistine ruler rather than a contradiction. Doeg is called an Edomite, a descendant of Esau from the land southeast of the Dead Sea, and his presence in Saul's service shows the king employing foreigners.
cultural:
The bread of the Presence was twelve loaves set out on a table in the sanctuary before the LORD each Sabbath. When they were replaced with fresh bread, the old loaves were holy food to be eaten by the priests in a holy place (Leviticus 24:5-9). Ahimelech's condition, that the young men had kept themselves from women, reflects the rule that sexual relations made a person ritually unclean until evening (Leviticus 15:18) and the practice of keeping soldiers ritually pure on campaign (Deuteronomy 23:9-10; compare 2 Samuel 11:11). Ahimelech bends the rule for the sake of hungry men, but he does not ignore it.

The ephod mentioned in verse 9 was the priestly garment used for seeking God's guidance, and Goliath's sword had been placed behind it as a trophy dedicated to the LORD. In the ancient world, captured weapons of a defeated enemy were often laid up in a sanctuary as a thanks offering for victory. David's pretended madness worked because the mentally disturbed were often treated with a mixture of fear and avoidance, and a raving man would not be considered a threat or a prize.
literary: The chapter is two short scenes linked by fear and deception. In the first, David lies to a priest; in the second, he performs madness before a king. The narrator slips a single sentence into the middle of the first scene, the note that Doeg the Edomite was there that day (verse 7), and says nothing more about him until chapter 22. That brief line is a deliberate delay, and a reader who notices it senses trouble. The Philistine servants' quotation of the women's song (verse 11) repeats 18:7 word for word, showing how far David's fame has spread and how it now endangers him. There is irony in David arriving at Gath with Goliath's sword, and in the servants calling him “the king of the land,” a title he does not yet hold.

outline.t: David receives the consecrated bread from Ahimelech
David feigns madness before Achish of Gath

doctrines.note: The bread was holy, and Ahimelech takes the rules about it seriously. Yet he gives it to hungry men, showing that the purpose of holy things is not undermined by meeting human need. Jesus later draws on this very story to make that point.
David's life is preserved at Gath not by a heroic act but by a humiliating performance. God's protection of his anointed does not always look dignified.

David's lie to Ahimelech seems small and practical, but it will cost the lives of the priests of Nob (22:22). The chapter shows how deception can have consequences far beyond what the deceiver intends.

words.note: Qodesh, holiness or holy thing. It describes the consecrated bread and, in David's reply, the equipment of the young men. Holiness in the Old Testament means being set apart for God, and it governed what could be eaten, touched, and by whom.

Panim, face or presence. The bread of the Presence is literally the bread of the face, set before the LORD's face in the sanctuary. The phrase expresses the idea that the LORD was present among his people and that they lived before him.

Shaga, to be mad or act insanely. It appears three times in Achish's complaint. Elsewhere the word can be used scornfully of prophets (2 Kings 9:11). David's survival depends on being seen as a madman, not a warrior.

Halal, in this form to act like a fool or madman. It is spelled like the verb meaning to praise (from which comes hallelujah), though lexicons usually treat it as a separate root with a different meaning. The heading of Psalm 34 remembers this moment, and that psalm is a song of praise for deliverance.

christ: Jesus refers to this chapter directly. When the Pharisees objected that his disciples were picking grain on the Sabbath, he reminded them that David and his companions ate the consecrated bread when they were hungry (Mark 2:23-28; Matthew 12:1-8; Luke 6:1-5). His point was that the law's purpose includes mercy toward human need, and that the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath. Jesus places himself in the position of David, the anointed but not yet enthroned king, whose followers are provided for even from holy things. The New Testament presents Jesus as the one who both honors God's holiness and fulfills the law's deepest intention of mercy.

hard.q: In Mark 2:26 Jesus connects this event with the high priesthood of Abiathar, but 1 Samuel names Ahimelech. Is this a contradiction?
hard.a: The difficulty is real and well known. Abiathar was Ahimelech's son, the one priest who escaped Saul's massacre in chapter 22 and later served David as high priest. Several explanations are offered. Some note that the Greek phrase in Mark can be read as a way of naming a section of Scripture by its best-known figure, much as Mark 12:26 refers to Moses' account of the bush by that heading. Others suggest the phrase means in the lifetime of Abiathar, who was present at Nob and became the better-known high priest. Some scholars conclude that Mark or his source simply named the more famous priest in error. Matthew and Luke, in their parallel accounts, do not name the priest at all. Readers of different convictions about Scripture weigh these explanations differently, but none affects the point Jesus was making from the story.

questions: David's lie to Ahimelech seemed harmless at the time. When have you seen a small deception lead to consequences you never intended?
Ahimelech gave holy bread to hungry men. How do you balance respect for sacred things with care for people in need?
The anointed king was reduced to pretending madness to stay alive. What does it mean to trust God's promises when your circumstances seem to contradict them?
